extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent agents/attorneys and patent examiners working on computer-implemented inventions in Canada
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and examining patent applications for computer-implemented inventions (claims, disclosure, enablement, novelty, obviousness, and statutory subject-matter) under the Canadian Patent Act and Patent Rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement of algorithms/flowcharts
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the algorithm or logic performed by the computer lie at the heart of the invention, a full description of the algorithm or logic tree should be provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the algorithm is described by a flow chart (a drawing), a written explanation of the flow chart is necessary to provide support for any claims that refer to the algorithm or logic. To successfully practice the invention, the person skilled in the art must be able to put each step in the flow chart into operation without recourse to inventive ingenuity or undue experimentation; the flow chart and any accompanying description must therefore provide any information necessary to enable the algorithm to be so practised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of written description relative to common general knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of written description necessary depends on the relationship of each step to the common general knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the algorithm invokes well-known operations, very little or no specific description may be necessary. If specific operations needed would not be obvious to the person skilled in the art, those operations must be fully described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding inoperative embodiments and misleading common knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: If common general knowledge would lead the skilled person to attempt to enable the algorithm in ways that would not work, the description should provide sufficient instructions to allow the person skilled in the art to arrive at operable embodiments and avoid inoperative ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide instructions or routes that lead to operable embodiments when the obvious approaches would fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of limited description
rubrics_metrics.description: Where limited description is provided, this is taken as an indication that the applicant considers that the selection of suitable means to perform the stated function would be readily apparent to a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may treat sparse disclosure as the applicant relying on common general knowledge; risk of insufficiency if that assumption is wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flowcharts require accompanying textual description
rubrics_metrics.description: Flow charts are diagrams with boxes and arrows representing states/steps; when they illustrate the algorithm of the invention, a written explanation is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on a flowchart alone to enable claims referencing the algorithm; include textual detail sufficient for practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source code versus pseudocode sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Source code or pseudocode may be provided but generally will not, by themselves, provide a full and enabling description of an invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Source code may be platform-dependent and not a clear, unambiguous description. Pseudocode (semi-structured natural language) usually has greater value than source code, but like flowcharts typically requires accompanying description; pseudocode alone will typically not be sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common general knowledge about programming
rubrics_metrics.description: The activities required to reduce logic instructions to computer code are considered part of the common general knowledge of a skilled programmer; typically it is not necessary to describe how to write computer code in general or for a specific language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the algorithm only invokes well-known operations, expressing commands as lines of code is not inventive. But if only broad terms are disclosed and it would not be clear to the skilled person what operations or logic are needed, disclosure is insufficient because the programmer would have to exercise ingenuity to design the program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (no anticipation by prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: A computer-implemented invention must not be anticipated by prior art relevant under section 28.2 of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be anticipatory, a single prior written disclosure, understood in light of common general knowledge, must both provide a written description of the claimed invention and sufficient instructions to enable practice by the skilled person without inventive effort or undue burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential elements for novelty/anticipation analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential elements of an invention are those that have a bearing on what the invention will do and how it does it (i.e., on its practical and promised utility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing to prior art, compare all essential elements; non-essential elements need not be considered for anticipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software commands as essential elements in device claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering a computer device (machine) claim, the effect of any commands being implemented by software must be considered to determine if they lead to a technological effect relevant to the promised utility of the device; if so, those commands are essential elements of the device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commands that merely apply functionality the machine already had are not essential; commands that change technological behavior are essential and must be included in novelty analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation by prior use/public availability (software)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior sale or use of an invention can amount to anticipation if it makes available information that describes the claimed invention and is enabling; publicly available software prior to the claim date can be prior art if it provides sufficient information to comprehend the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The information made available must be such that the skilled person could write a clear and unambiguous description of the claimed invention; prior art software that achieves the same function could be anticipatory for broad functional claims, whereas for method-specific claims it must be shown the same method was used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse engineering as evidence for anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability of the skilled person to reverse engineer a product (e.g., decompiling software) in accordance with known analytical techniques may be relevant to whether a publicly available product anticipates a claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary to show that reverse engineering actually occurred—only that it would be possible without inventive effort to ascertain the method implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant grace period
rubrics_metrics.description: In considering whether anticipation by prior sale or use has occurred, the grace period provided in paragraph 28.2(1)(a) of the Patent Act applies in respect of any making available of the invention by the applicant or by a person who obtained the relevant knowledge directly or indirectly from the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-disclosure by applicant within the statutory grace period may avoid anticipation objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness (ingenuity) standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness is evaluated in view of the overall state of the art contained in the prior art, when considered as a whole in light of the common general knowledge of the person skilled in the art; a claimed invention must be the result of ingenuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claimed invention is obvious if prior art teachings, when combined, would lead to the claimed invention and it would be uninventive (obvious) to combine them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-essential elements do not contribute inventiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing inventive in adding a non-essential element to an invention, since by definition the non-essential element is irrelevant to the invention's successful operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus novelty/obviousness analysis on essential elements only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automation of manual processes tends toward obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: It is considered obvious that computers can be used to automate many manual operations; the idea of automating a manual process is, absent reasons to the contrary, considered to be uninventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To support claims to computer-automated versions of known manual methods, the inventive step typically must be found in the solution to specific challenges attendant to enabling the automation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step via combination achieving new unitary result
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a computer-implemented invention aims to achieve a new unitary result through use of a combination of known hardware and software, an inventive step may exist by virtue of recognizing that the combination will achieve that result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using the hardware & software together merely results in a predictable outcome, the alleged invention is a mere aggregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must fit a statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject-matter of a claim must belong to a category of invention as defined in section 2 of the Patent Act; elements used to define the subject-matter must be of a type appropriate to that category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mixing elements from different categories in a way that creates ambiguity about intended subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-implemented method claim clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim is directed to a method to be implemented in whole or in part by computer, it must be unambiguously clear which steps of the method are being carried out by the computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifying 'computer-implemented' implies some steps are by computer but does not force a presumption; avoid steps that could be performed by either a person or a computer without clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine (computer) claim must define physical components
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim is directed to a machine, it must be defined in terms of physical components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means statements are common but if interpreted as software they must be specified as stored on physical memory either in the claim or description; language should be clear, concise and unambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: System claims require unambiguous meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'system' may refer to a machine, a computer program or a method depending on context; care must be taken to ensure its intended meaning is unambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In computer arts, absent other indication it may be presumed to mean a machine; where not a machine, explicitly define category to comply with subsection 27(4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Software product claim form and preamble wording
rubrics_metrics.description: A computer program per se is considered an abstract scheme, plan or set of rules and not an invention; under certain circumstances software can be claimed by directing the claim to a physical memory storing the computer program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble 'a physical memory having stored thereon...' directs claim to statutory embodiment (manufacture), whereas 'a computer program stored on a physical memory' directs to a computer program (excluded). It must be explicitly defined that the computer program is present as machine-executable code; only machine-executable code can change the technological functionality of the physical memory. Non-executable code is mere descriptive matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software-modified physical memory as statutory subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the computer program would cause the device it controls to provide a technological solution to a technological problem, the 'software-modified physical memory' is a single discrete element and can be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the program is novel and inventive and causes technological effect, both the programmed device and the physical memory storing the executable code may be statutory and allowable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means statements support and specificity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Means statements (defining a part of an invention by function rather than specific structure) are not objectionable per se, provided the claim meets all requirements of the Patent Act and Patent Rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The description must describe what types of means are contemplated unless this would be obvious to the skilled person; where it would not be obvious which means fall within the scope, the claim may be defective for lack of support or indefiniteness. Means statements may refer to hardware or software and context should clarify which.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed claim types and category-appropriate elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim in one category (e.g., a machine) defines its subject-matter in terms of elements from another category (e.g., method steps), there is a risk of ambiguity over the intended subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A machine claim must define structural components that distinguish it from other machines. A method-of-using-device claim must include at least one step applying the device. Product-by-process claims define a product by its process of production and are not a format for defining a product in terms of the method for which it will be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical user interfaces (GUI) generally non-statutory
rubrics_metrics.description: The term GUI refers to the arrangement of visual elements displayed on a screen and is considered information; a GUI as such is subject to non-statutory treatment as descriptive matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features having purely intellectual or aesthetic significance are not statutory and cannot provide a statutory contribution. The specific visual arrangement is not patentable where it does not provide a technological solution to a practical problem. However, a GUI integrated with statutory subject matter (i.e., that provides a technological solution to a technological problem) may be patentable if novel and inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data structures treated as abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: A data structure is a format for organizing related data items and is considered by the Office to be an abstract idea or plan; a data structure per se is disembodied and not an invention within section 2 of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a data structure to impact patentability it must in some way limit the technological nature of a statutory element in the claim (e.g., contribute to a technological solution).
